In traditional Christian and alchemical iconography, the pelican was believed to wound her own breast to feed her starving young with her blood. Here, it serves as a powerful symbol for the alchemical process of "multiplication" and the self-sacrifice required to achieve the "Great Work." 

The bird stands upon a golden crescent moon, representing the "lunar" or silver stage of alchemy, which rests on a square heraldic base. This base is marked with a saltire (an X-shaped cross) and four red roses, symbols often associated with the Rosicrucian movement. Divine light descends from a sun-like source at the top, suggesting that the "Hermetic Philosophy" is a path to spiritual enlightenment.</note>

### To
## Johann Valentin Andreae.

---

In your **Calw** — you were once so content there,
O immortalized one! and only the beckoning of the Divine
Tore you away from your valley, where you
Harvested the fruits of your labor. <note>Andreae spent his most productive years in Calw (1620–1639), where he founded the "Calwer Färberkasse," one of the first social insurance systems in Germany.</note>
You do not journey to Stuttgart out of pride —
No! only with your gaze fixed upon a higher goal,
To become for the Fatherland what you were for
->**Calw** —<-

A promoter of good morals and true Christianity!
Yet envy, hatred, and greed
Often strewed your path with thorns.
There, almost every year, you strengthened yourself
In the embrace of your Calw, at the spring of Teinach, <note>Teinach's spring refers to the mineral baths in Bad Teinach, a popular retreat near Calw where Andreae sought physical and spiritual restoration.</note>
For new battles with the vipers. <note>original: "Nattern"; a metaphor for the critics and courtly rivals who opposed Andreae's reform efforts in Stuttgart.</note>

# Preface.
---

Shortly after the first volume of these **autobiographies** was printed, the life story of the famous **Gibbon**, <note>Edward Gibbon (1737–1794), the English historian best known for *The History of the Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire*.</note> written by himself, appeared (*); and I was already making preparations to announce it as the second part of this collection. However, before I could even come to an agreement with the publisher regarding this, two other bookstores had already undertaken the **translation**.

What **Herder** <note>Johann Gottfried von Herder (1744–1803), a philosopher and critic who argued that biographies were essential for understanding the "spirit" of an age.</note> and others [have said] regarding the utility of such self-authored biographies

---
(*) *Miscellaneous Works of Edward Gibbon, Esq., with Memoirs of his Life and Writings composed by himself.* London. Vol. I. II. 1796. Compare with Schubart’s *English Leaves* <note>original: "Englische Blätter"; a contemporary German journal that introduced English literature and culture to German readers.</note> Volume 6, Issues 3 and 4.

<meta>catchword: ge- (likely leading to "gesagt" or "geurtheilt" / "said" or "judged")</meta>

said, is confirmed by a passage in *Gibbon’s* works. “A sincere and simple narrative of my life’s circumstances—he says—may perhaps grant me many a cheerful hour, but it will perhaps not unjustly expose me to the suspicion of vanity. However, the experience of past and present times shows that the public is always uncommonly eager to get to know those men closely who have left behind a monument of their spirit. The most insignificant reports about such men are collected with care and read with zeal, and students in all subjects are accustomed to using a way of life for doctrine and instruction that so closely approaches their own. To all appearances, my name will in time be added to the thousand articles of the *Bibliographia Britannica* <note>The *Biographia Britannica* was a massive multi-volume biographical dictionary of notable British figures; Gibbon anticipates his own inclusion among the historical greats.</note>: and so it remains certain that no one else is as capable as I of recording the series of my thoughts and actions. <meta>This page continues the preface by the editor, who is quoting Edward Gibbon’s defense of autobiography. Gibbon argues that the memoirs of great individuals are often the most valuable portions of their literary legacies, providing a precedent for his own self-narrative.</meta>

XI

Hume’s <note>original: "Hume's"; referring to the philosopher David Hume, whose brief autobiography *My Own Life* (1776) was highly regarded for its concise honesty.</note> example could excuse my undertaking. However, it would not be difficult to list here a long series of ancient and modern authors who have left behind their own portraits in various forms. Such portraits are often the most interesting—indeed, sometimes the only attractive—part of their writings; and as long as they are written sincerely and honestly, we rarely complain about the detail and precision of such memoirs. The life stories of Pliny the Younger <note>A Roman lawyer and author whose letters provide a window into the social and political life of the 1st century AD.</note>, Petrarch <note>The 14th-century Italian poet and scholar whose letters were central to the development of Humanism.</note>, and Erasmus <note>Desiderius Erasmus, the great Renaissance humanist whose extensive correspondence documented the intellectual shifts of the Reformation era.</note> are very attractively expressed in the letters they left to the world. The essays <note>original: "Versuche"; a reference to the literary genre of the 'Essay' established by Montaigne.</note> of Montaigne and William Temple <note>Sir William Temple (1628–1699), an English diplomat and essayist admired for his prose style.</note> lead us, as it were, into the innermost chamber and the sanctuary of their authors' souls. We smile without contempt at the stubborn passions of Benvenuto Cellini <note>A Florentine sculptor and goldsmith whose autobiography is famous for its colorful tales of brawls and artistic triumphs.</note>, and the droll follies of Colley Cibber <note>An English actor-manager and Poet Laureate; his memoirs were often mocked for their vanity but praised for their theatrical history.</note>. The confessions of Rousseau and Saint Augustine <note>Referring to the *Confessions* of both Jean-Jacques Rousseau (1782) and St. Augustine of Hippo (c. 400 AD), which revolutionized the exploration of the inner self.</note> unlock for us the most secret windings of the human heart; the commentaries of the lea- <note>The word "ge-lehr..." (learned) is split here by the page break.</note>

XII

the learned Huet’s <note>Pierre-Daniel Huet (1630–1721), a French bishop and scholar. While he wrote massive theological works, his personal memoirs are often more highly regarded by later historians.</note> [writings] have long outlived his *Gospel Demonstration* <note>original: "Demonstrationem Evangelicam"; a major work of Christian apologetics published in 1679.</note>; and the memoirs of Goldoni <note>Carlo Goldoni (1707–1793), a famous Italian playwright whose memoirs are a primary source for the history of the theater.</note> contain far more genuine dramatic spirit than his Italian comedies. The heretic and the clergyman are very strikingly expressed in the life and character of Whiston <note>William Whiston (1667–1752), an English theologian and mathematician who was famously expelled from Cambridge for his "heretical" views on the Trinity.</note> and Bishop Newton <note>Thomas Newton (1704–1782), an English cleric whose autobiography provides a detailed account of the ecclesiastical politics of his day.</note>; and even the follies of Michel de Marolles <note>A 17th-century French abbot known for his massive collection of prints and his somewhat eccentric translations.</note> and Anthony Wood <note>An English antiquary (1632–1695) known for his meticulous and often grumpy diaries about life at Oxford University.</note> gain an uncommon interest through the faithful depiction of people and customs.

Since Gibbon <note>referring to Edward Gibbon, whose memoirs the editor had likely just finished translating or studying before turning to this project.</note> had now been taken from me, it occurred to me—on the occasion when June 27th in my historical pocket-calendar reminded me of J. V. Andreä <note>Johann Valentin Andreä (1586–1654), the subject of this book. He was a prominent German theologian and social reformer.</note>—that his autobiography was still unprinted. I therefore turned to Pastor Burk in Weiltingen, who shared his very accurate transcript with me with the most friendly readiness—at that time, I still knew nothing of the existence of the original manuscript, which was later occasionally compared [to the transcript]—for which I express my public thanks to him here.

<meta>This page continues the editor’s preface, moving from the general value of memoirs to the specific challenges of translating Johann Valentin Andreä’s autobiography from its original Latin. XIII

As difficult as the style of Andreas—which is indeed sometimes convoluted—his antitheses, his peculiar train of thought, and so forth, made the translation, it was at times a task like that of the literary reformers <note>A reference to Renaissance humanists who worked to recover and edit classical Greek and Latin texts.</note> who translated an as-yet-unprinted Greek author from manuscripts that were not entirely correct; yet I nevertheless undertook it with love. I did so because the gradually developing image of the man pleased me, and I learned to increasingly value the integrity of his intentions, his unshakable courage in the most oppressive situations, and his perseverance through often failed efforts. How many others would have lost heart <note>literally: "let their hands sink"</note> if, instead of the reward—which every true patriot <note>In the 18th-century sense: one who is devoted to the welfare of their community or people.</note> seeks only within themselves, not in external things—they saw themselves further persecuted and slandered! Indeed, nowhere is Andreä greater than under the most adverse circumstances. In a city entirely burned to the ground, surrounded by public and secret enviers and enemies, hindered at every step, without his own shelter, and almost without pay, he feeds, clothes,

<note>original German vocabulary: Andreas, translation, literary reformers, patriot, courage, developed</note>

provides for many thousands of his fellow citizens, even strangers! What did he not do for the <term>theological seminary</term> <note>The "Stift" in Tübingen, a famous Protestant residence and school for training clergy where Andreä served.</note> here! What for the <term>Gymnasium</term> <note>A classical secondary school; specifically the Eberhard-Ludwigs-Gymnasium in Stuttgart.</note> in Stuttgart! What for the social morals, which became increasingly corrupt with the progress of the Thirty Years’ War, <note>A series of devastating conflicts in Central Europe (1618–1648) that caused immense population loss and social collapse.</note> instead of the people being led toward piety by the general misfortune! What more might he have achieved if he had been allowed to work according to the full scope of his activity! How often was I tempted to wish, along with Spener: <note>Philipp Jakob Spener (1635–1705), a later influential theologian known as the "father of Pietism."</note> “Oh! if only I could awaken him, or men like him!” How necessary such true Württembergers would be in a state where no community spirit and no pure patriotism exist—despite our excellent constitution, which only requires a few improvements based on moderate principles—but where instead egoism, nepotism, (*) party spirit, etc., largely prevail! — but back to the work itself!

<meta>This page continues the editor’s explanation of his editorial choices in presenting Johann Valentin Andreä’s life. The previous page ended with the editor shifting focus "back to the work itself!" and the catchword was "I," leading into "I gave it..."</meta>

XV

I gave it exactly as I found it. However, the fact that I did not include the <term>promotions</term> <note>Academic appointments or advancements in rank within the church or school system.</note> recorded in **Bebenhausen** <note>A former Cistercian monastery near Tübingen that served as a prominent Protestant cloister school where Andreä held office.</note>, especially in the final books; that I do not recount the changes regarding his scribes or the maids; and that I also made no mention of the lapdogs he received from Augsburg—for this, every reader will forgive me who wishes to get to know the man himself, rather than learn of every domestic incident. While I was unmerciful toward the two **Bolognese dogs** <note>A breed of small lapdogs popular among the nobility and clergy in the 17th century.</note>, *Little Heart* and *Lucky*, I nevertheless allowed the courageous male pigeon (*) to keep its place, partly because the circumstance seemed curious from a natural history perspective, and partly to paint my hero’s weakness with a single stroke: namely, that he occasionally considered things concerning himself to be more interesting than they actually were. For I dare as little to declare him entirely free from a certain dose of vanity as I do from an attachment to some superstitious opinions of his age; likewise, an undeniable—and not always well-founded—sullenness and ill-humor in his final years is evident.

---

(*) P. 277.

I will mention one more circumstance here which Andreä himself (†) did not develop quite clearly. It seems, namely, that during his first theological examination held in the year 1612, the authorities were not entirely satisfied with his dogmatic knowledge, and he was therefore advised to return to the **Seminary in Tübingen** <note>The *Evangelisches Stift Tübingen*, a famous theological college in Württemberg.</note> for a while longer. # Postscript.

### regarding page 253.

Regarding the aforementioned **Stirzel**, I have only now found the following note in Zapf’s *Remarkable Findings from his Library* <note>original: "Zapfs Merkwürdigkeiten seiner Bibliothek"</note>, part 2, page 282. “Stirzel was born in Augsburg on April 12, 1591. His teacher in his home city was **David Höschel**. In the year 1609, he studied in Jena; in 1611, in Tübingen; and in 1613, in Altdorf. It is not known how he came to Rotenburg an der Tauber. Here he found his fortune, becoming a **Councilman** <note>original: <term>Rathsherr</term></note> in 1624, and finally **Mayor** <note>original: <term>Bürgermeister</term></note>, **Consistorial Assessor** <note>original: <term>Konsistorialbeisizer</term>; a member of a church court.</note>, and **School Superintendent** <note>original: <term>Scholarche</term></note>; he died on April 7, 1668. See also Freher’s *Theater* <note>original: <term>Theatr.</term></note>, page 1184. The aforementioned scholar possesses a collection of 400 letters that he wrote to various friends and had likely intended for publication. None of these is addressed to Andreä.”

### regarding page 327.

Among the oratorical exercises of the **Count of Castell**, the following small book also belongs: *Wolfgang Georg, Count and Lord of Castell’s Deliberation on the best method of acquiring wealth and the use of that which is acquired. Held in the Illustrious College in the year of Christ 1626. Tübingen, printed by Brunn. 12mo.* <note>original: "Wolf. Georgi Com. ac Dom. in Castell Consultatio de optimo parandarum opum modo & partarum usu. Habita in Ill. Collegio An. Chr. MDCXXVI. Tub. typis Brunnianis. 12."</note>

### of Brunswick-Lüneburg (*)

---

->To the Most Serene Prince and<-
->Lord, Lord<-
->August,<-
->Duke of Brunswick and Lüneburg,<-

Before You, Most Serene and most powerful Duke! one of the magnates of Germany, I appear, a German man; before the Lutheran prince, a Lutheran theo- <note>The word is likely "theologian" (Theologe), interrupted by the page break.</note>

Nothing in my whole life was of greater concern to me than that I—from my earliest years—compared the **Protestant religion** <note>original: "evangelische Religion"; specifically referring to the Lutheran faith.</note>, which the great Luther freed from darkness and which I myself drew in with my mother’s milk, with the **Holy Scriptures**; that I supplemented it from the unadulterated **Augsburg Confession** <note>The primary confession of faith of the Lutheran Church, written in 1530.</note> and the **Formula of Concord** <note>A definitive doctrinal agreement of the Lutheran Church from 1577 intended to settle internal disputes.</note> to understand it more fully; that I confirmed it through the instruction of my teachers, especially **Dr. Matthias Hafenreffer** <note>A prominent Lutheran theologian (1561–1619) at Tübingen who was Andreä's mentor.</note>; strengthened it by reading our theologians and observing the agreement of the **Holy Fathers** <note>The influential early Christian theologians of the first few centuries after Christ.</note>; and finally, for about thirty years—according to the testimony of so many listeners and respected colleagues—publicly professed it in the presence of the Court, the Chancellery, and the University, while detesting its opponents. 

Nevertheless, I could not tame the barking of **slander**, which attacked me either through secret whispers or public accusations, and blamed me for being infected by the very **heresies** for which I had the strongest loathing, or for secret collusion, or at least for bordering upon them.

# First Book.
## From the Year 1586 to 1614.
### Introduction.

Whether I once walked among mortals, and who I was among the lower rank of men, likely matters little to posterity. To have possessed life and the use of sound reason <note>In this context, "sound reason" (gesunder Vernunft) refers to the 17th-century ideal of a mind capable of both logical thought and moral discernment.</note> through God’s grace, and to have been called by Jesus Christ to a better life and a blessed eternity—while meanwhile being useful to Church and State according to the gifts and guidance of the Holy Spirit, and moreover being favored with many earthly and heavenly blessings—this must be more than enough for us. Yet, because it is the nature of human memory to linger for at least a while among the living after death, and to find belief according to whatever tongue or pen it is assigned—whether one chooses out of love to exalt the small, or out of envy to diminish what is greater, or whether a flamboyant style of writing intentionally deceives the credulity of men—it seems, then, not to be a matter of indifference whether a biographer harms our innocence or flatters our faults; on the contrary, it is good if, regarding our good and bad actions, insofar as they

<meta>This page continues the Introduction to Book One, following Johann Valentin Andreae's argument for why an autobiography is necessary. It picks up mid-sentence from the previous page, discussing the preservation of a "genuine narrative" to counter biased historical accounts.</meta>

...are worthy of remembrance, a genuine narrative exists.

Since the hatred between different religions, the spirit of various factions, and private feuds can sometimes be so harmful even to great virtue—with one side offering as much praise as the other heaps on blame—one often has good reason to doubt whom to believe. Many would rather delay their judgment of a person, or leave the final verdict to God, than be subject to the passions and biases of others.

For these reasons, some people, guided by a clear conscience and free from hatred or bias, have decided to describe the course of their own lives and leave behind a sincere account of their convictions. They feared that a stranger’s brush <note>A metaphor for a biographer’s artistic license or lack of personal insight.</note> might paint them inaccurately—perhaps the faction they detested would praise them, or the group they were devoted to would fail to recognize them as one of their own. Indeed, they worried that neither side might truly know them, and that a "purchased pen" <note>original: "erkaufte Feder"; referring to a writer hired to produce a specific, often flattering or slanderous, narrative.</note> might display them to the world’s various judgments like a spectacle in a public square.

A different reason drove me to attempt something similar. For almost my entire life—unlike that of many others—has not flowed in a straight line, but rather through various...

Picking up from the previous page's metaphor of life as a winding river, Andreae moves from justifying the act of writing to defining his own style: one of plain, honest sincerity rather than polished rhetoric.</meta>

...windings, sometimes overflowing, sometimes nearly drying up, and running now clear, now turbid—I believe I am doing a good thing by presenting this account of my person. I intend to distance myself from all passions <note>original: "Leidenschaften"</note> and the artificial makeup of eloquence <note>original: "Schminke der Beredsamkeit"; a common 17th-century metaphor for deceptive or overly flowery rhetoric.</note>, and instead write with genuine German fidelity <note>original: "ächter deutscher Treue"; a cultural trope signifying plain-spoken honesty and sincerity.</note>. Neither unearned praise nor unmerited blame shall be gathered here; I do not seek to immortalize the memory of great services to the state <note>original: "Staat"</note>. Instead, the reader shall simply be presented with the image of a life that has been as short as it has been distressed and unfortunate on all sides.

Here, any reader may observe and pity so many various errors, changes, and storms—so many obstacles, injustices, slanders, and schemes—along with the struggles, anxieties, illnesses, and sad misfortunes. At the same time, the reader may compare these scenes with the diary of their own pilgrimage <note>original: "Wanderschaft"; the concept of life as a journey or spiritual wandering.</note>, while also admiring the goodness of God <note>original: "Güte Gottes"</note>. Without Him, the slender thread of my life would not have endured, but would have been in danger of snapping in every storm.

Those who are more closely acquainted with the course of my life and my studies will easily be satisfied with me. However, those who do not know me, and who have allowed themselves to be led by the judgments of others or by their own lack of discernment, have persecuted me greatly. Furthermore, the freedom of my spirit <note>original: "Freiheit meines Geistes"</note>, my tongue, and my judgment <note>original: "Urtheil"</note> has so offended many that some...

<summary>Andreae declares his intent to write a plain, honest account of his troubled life, eschewing flowery rhetoric to focus on his personal hardships and God's providence. He acknowledges that his outspoken nature and intellectual independence have earned him many enemies.</summary>

...did not even want to believe that I belong to the Lutheran religion <note>original: "Luthersche Religion"; referring to the Evangelical-Lutheran confession, which was central to Andreae’s identity as a theologian.</note>, which I have nevertheless sincerely professed throughout my entire life; instead, they weighed me down through the burden of resentment <note>original: "Mißgunst"</note>, suspicion, slander, and hatred. Through this, they may silence the mouths of the malicious and protect my memory from injustice, or better inform the ignorant and the gullible. Above all, they shall be able to testify: I have neither been unfaithful to the religion and virtue of my father and grandfather, nor have I been a disgrace to my family, nor have I been entirely useless to the Christian Church.

<meta>This page continues the autobiographical account of Johann Valentin Andreae. While the previous page listed his formal schoolteachers in Königsbronn, this page shifts to his private tutors at home, who were hired primarily as medical assistants for his ailing father.</meta>

But as my father was afflicted by various illnesses, he took two <note>original: "Schlesier"</note> Silesians, **Johannes Moller** and **Johannes Hartig**—both devoted to the <term>medical arts: "Arzneikunst," referring here to both pharmacy and general medical practice.</term>—into his home to have medical assistance. He employed them both for the preparation of medicines and for the instruction of his son. They performed both duties with great faithfulness. However, the latter <note>referring to Hartig</note> showed the greatest and most successful diligence in this second area. To him, I confess, I owe a great deal more than to my other teachers.

It is impossible to describe the vast difference between a capable teacher and an incapable one. **Hartig** was more concise, yet his instruction was exceptional and remained effective throughout my entire life. Others taught with more conscientiousness than with true scholarship <note>original: "wissenschaftlich"; here implying a methodical or academic depth rather than just following a routine.</note>. I do not reproach them—they all deserve my gratitude—but I only lament that so very few people truly understand how to shape and teach the young. 

And yet, such an office is often entrusted, without much selection, almost exclusively to the most inexperienced! Consequently, time, resources, and even the strokes <note>a reference to the corporal punishment common in 16th-century schooling</note> are squandered, so that a talented mind—if he does not work his own way out of the mire—feels himself sinking deeper rather than being pulled out. What I should claim for myself, I do not know. Out of impatience with such frequent delays, I surrendered...

Nevertheless, I shall carry the marks of that twisting for the rest of my life.

With these, I joined Zwinger’s *Theater* (*), which is distinguished as much by its select method as by its infinite historical variety, and upon which I spent many a night hour. For I had so divided my time that I dedicated the day to the sciences, but dedicated the time for reading authors deep into the night. My petition was in vain; indeed, I was even forbidden from hoping for a position in my homeland. Therefore, I gradually slackened in my study of theology and began to [look] toward another way of life...

<meta>This page continues Johann Valentin Andreä’s autobiographical reflections from around 1610-1620. Johann Truchseß <note>Johann (Hans) Truchseß von Waldburg (1552–1620), the father of Andreä's pupils and a significant patron for the author</note>, as he was already approaching old age, suffered from a suppuration <term>Vereiterung: A chronic, pus-producing infection, likely a severe renal abscess in this context</term> of one of the kidneys. Despite all the physicians and medicines, his loins rotted so severely that a large wound opened there, and one could see the internal organs. The affliction was great, long-lasting, and accompanied by such pain that many wondered how he could remain alive. Otherwise, the man was not wicked, but he had been somewhat negligent in matters of religion. Now he turned to pious contemplations and devoted himself to prayer. For since everyone despaired of his recovery, he sustained himself only through faith in God and fervent prayer, and began to comfort himself and hope for better things for himself. Now he rejected all human help and relied on God alone, awaiting His assistance with incredible patience, and finally received it. Through this, from a careless man he became a very zealous one; he did not cease to praise the comfort one draws from religion and the efficacy of prayer. Therefore, as a memorial, he had the chapel of his castle, which until then had been unadorned, decorated and painted. I saw this myself when I visited the good man for the last time at Krespach <note>Kressbach Castle, located near Tübingen, which served as a residence for the Waldburg family</note> in the year 1620. I marveled at how much better he had become—from an already good man into someone even better—through the beneficial cross <term>wohlthätige Kreuz: A theological concept, particularly in Lutheranism, where suffering is viewed as a "cross" sent by God to refine and improve the believer's character</term>, and soon after I lost him to a peaceful death.

During my stay in **Geneva**, I noticed something very important, which I shall forget as little as I shall long for it my whole life through. Besides the perfect form of a free state, the Republic possesses a special ornament and a house of discipline in the <term>Sittengericht: The Consistory, a church court composed of elders and pastors responsible for maintaining public morality and ecclesiastical order</term>, which weekly investigates the conduct of the citizens, even the smallest excesses—first through the overseers in the city districts, then by the elders, and finally by the Senate itself, as the gravity of the matter or the hardness of heart and stubbornness of the perpetrator may necessitate. Such **purity of morals** <note>original: "Sittenreinigkeit"</note> adorns the Christian religion quite extraordinarily; it is fitting and inherent to it, so that we cannot weep enough for its absence among us, and all upright people should work toward its restoration. Had the difference of religion not distanced me from **Geneva**, the harmony of its customs would have bound me to this city forever. Therefore, from that time on, I took every pains to introduce something similar into our own churches. 

Just as the entire state was ordered, so too the household of **Scaron**, where I took my meals, had an appearance of modesty. For constant prayer, reading of Holy Scripture, honorability in speech and actions, in dress and diet, and also temperance were its ornaments, so that I lived no less innocently there than in my father's house.

From **Geneva** I traveled to **Lyon** in the company of **Theodat** <note>Jean Diodati (1576–1649), the Genevan theologian previously mentioned, who was then traveling to raise funds for the city</note>, the clergyman, who was very proficient in the German language besides many others, and who was to gather a collection. My childhood was subject to illnesses; my youth, following the lot of orphans, was exposed to servitude and poverty; the period that followed was entangled in various and arduous labors, as well as travels. Fortune was, for the most part, a stepmother <note>A common historical idiom meaning that fate was harsh, unkind, or neglectful, rather than nurturing.</note> to me, and my relatives were harsher than strangers; yet support was granted by friends, and my spirit was strengthened for every fate. Without warm tears and humble sighs, I would not have tasted my current happiness so well. Therefore, I owe my God the greatest thanks: that He imposed moderation upon me through physical suffering; that through the delicacy of pure feeling He preserved my chastity unblemished; and that at the same time He kept me free from the shackles of marriage—which were intended for me four times—dampened my excesses through lack, mixed bitterness into my curiosity, and snatched me from so many dangers of life and fortune. According to my belief and that of others, I thank the pious and fervent prayers of my mother for this grace of God with a willing heart.

## Second Book.
### From the Years 1614—1620.

---

### Deaconry in Vaihingen.

Instead of the journey to the Netherlands—which I intended to undertake upon the recommendation of Count Philipp of Oetingen to Margrave Joachim Ernst of Anspach—I instead moved in the month of March to Vaihingen, where my kind relative, Director Johann Walch, <note>Dr. Johann Ludwig Walch, Director from the years 1611–1616.</note> had secured the call <note>In a clerical context, a "call" refers to a formal invitation to take up a church office.</note> for me. At first, I took my meals with the Superintendent <term>Superintendent: A high-ranking Lutheran cleric who oversees the pastors of a specific district.</term>, Melchior Bengel, an honest man who was very well-disposed toward me. Since he possessed a considerable library, I was permitted to browse through it during the leisure I then enjoyed, and I supplemented what was lacking in my own collection. On the second of August, however, I joined myself in a continually happy marriage to Agnes Elisabeth, a daughter of Josua Grüninger, pastor at Poppenweiler. Erasmus Grüninger, the brother of my father-in-law <term>Schwäher: An archaic German term for a father-in-law.</term>, who was then the Abbot of Maulbronn <note>Maulbronn is a former Cistercian monastery; after the Reformation, it became a prestigious Protestant seminary.</note>, was present. From that time on, he refuted those who brought me into ill repute because of my travels, or who criticized me for [turning away] from the secular—

<meta>This page continues Johann Valentin Andreae's defense of his satirical writing style. He explains that his use of wit and irony in his book "Menippus" was intended as a "cure" for the ills of the church, though he admits his youthful approach may have been overly provocative.</meta>

The first to quiet the grumbling against me was Wilhelm von Remchingen, High Court Judge <note>A high-ranking legal official in the ducal court of Württemberg.</note>, a man of whom I cannot decide whether the blamelessness of his character, his scholarship, his knowledge of the world, or the prestige of his birth ennobles him more. Through the dedication of my *Christian Citizen* (*) I have in some measure repaid my debt of gratitude to him; since the year before, the *Stranger* (**), dedicated to Besold, had been wandering about, and the *Christian Freedom* (†), concerning the good cause and the *Praise of Theology*, had appeared under Hohenfelder's patronage.

The noble assessors of the High Court <note>Judicial officials who assisted the presiding judge.</note>, namely Burkhard Weiler, Johann Heinrich Offenburg, and Heinrich Schilling, followed the example set by Remchingen. Furthermore, Bidenbach <note>Likely Felix Bidenbach (1564–1612), a prominent Württemberg theologian and court preacher.</note> showed me a loyalty that had been proven in misfortune; being less subject to strict discipline, he could easily take my danger upon himself. Around this time, beyond all my expectations, it happened that the man whom I had long admired for his gifted genius and unusual erudition, the noble Georg Achatz Enenkel, Baron of Hohenegg <note>Georg Achatz Enenkel (1573–1620) was a prominent Austrian Protestant nobleman, historian, and diplomat known for his scholarship.</note>, voluntarily offered me his friendship and requested mine through a very beautiful letter. It is as follows:

->Greetings to you in Christ!<-

That nothing is more lovable than virtue, and that it entices people toward a mutual love—since, as Cicero <note>Referring to Marcus Tullius Cicero's famous treatise *De Amicitia* (On Friendship), which argues that true friendship is based on virtue.</note> says, through virtue we love even those whom we have never seen—that, I would say, has happened to me regarding you, if I had not already come to know your "better part" (that is, your heart, which is adorned with exceptional scholarship, judgment, and sincerity) through your writings. As soon as I knew you, I loved you, and I wished to be loved by you in return and to be received as an intimate friend. Just as I have now decided to take the first step, I would have done so long ago had not—I know not what—something made the path to you feel uncertain and difficult. I come to you, therefore, through our famous mutual friend Besold <note>Christoph Besold (1577–1638), a renowned jurist and polymath at the University of Tübingen, who was a mentor to Andreä and a central figure in his intellectual circle.</note>. # Book Three.
### From the year 1620—1630.

->The first decade in Calw.<-

Thus I was released from Vaihingen and came to Calw, a town on the Nagold <note>The Nagold is the river that flows through the heart of Calw in the northern Black Forest.</note>, famous for its wool-working <note>The wool trade and the later "Calw Wool-trading Company" were the backbones of the town's economy, making it one of the wealthiest towns in Württemberg.</note>, and, in respect of the friendliness and harmony of its citizens, the exact opposite of Vaihingen! I arrived there on March 5th, and on the 12th, following a sermon by the Abbot, Dr. Paul Rucker of Hirsau <note>Hirsau was a nearby former Benedictine monastery; after the Reformation, its leaders retained the title of "Abbot" or "Prelate" while serving as high-ranking Protestant officials.</note>—a man I never name without reverence—I was installed by him into my office. I had already brought my family there beforehand in a poor procession, not entirely without being mocked for it <note>Andreä likely arrived with very few possessions after his difficult years in Vaihingen, attracting some ridicule from onlookers.</note>.

My first concern was to follow in the footsteps of my predecessors, especially Johann Eckhover, who for about 40 years had cultivated the vineyard of the Lord <note>A common biblical metaphor for the pastoral care of a Christian congregation.</note> with much fruit, and to now undertake for the cause of Christianity that which I had found lacking in others. <meta>This page continues Johann Valentin Andreä’s reflections on the moral and financial state of his community in Calw. But almost beyond my strength, I was distressed by the fickleness and faithlessness of some men of our clerical order <term>geistlicher Stand: the body of ordained ministers and church officials</term>, with which they either adapted themselves to the circumstances of the times, or eagerly seized the opportunity of the now less strict church discipline <term>Kirchenzucht: the system of moral oversight and ecclesiastical rules governing the conduct of the community</term>. That they did not betray Christ’s flock <note>original: "Christi Heerde"; the congregation</note>, or even lead it to ruin, was only due to the indecisiveness of the enemies. For they themselves were ready to do the worst, and to permit it to their own people. Now they feign improvement, and are afraid of the rescue shimmering in the distance. But I, whom they considered a mere shadow-play <note>original: "Schattenspiel"; Andreä suggests they viewed him as a powerless figurehead or a mere illusion of authority</note>, have not yet forgotten everything. Yet several also remained faithful to their duties—namely to faith, patience, moderation, uprightness, obedience, contempt for earthly things, and even determination unto death—and may Jesus Christ continue to preserve them. If that peace, which is promised with so much pomp, does not deceive our hope, then the reward for the righteous—though admittedly only a few escaped the downfall—and the punishment for the wicked will not fail to appear.

Now I return to our alms <note>charitable relief funds for the poor</note>. For the Bavarian garrison <note>original: "Standquartier"; referring to the occupying military forces during the Thirty Years' War</note>, under the leadership of Johann Puks, did not hesitate—besides the many insults and more than barbaric arrogance inflicted upon us—to scrape out and suck dry our few remaining possessions. On June 1st, this rabble departed, followed by an occupation under Ensign <term>Fähndrich: the lowest rank of commissioned officer, responsible for carrying the troop's banner</term> Andreas Schumann, who was not much more humane or restrained. Besieged by such "guests," I did not travel even an hour’s distance from the city all year; indeed—if one is permitted to joke during such a sorrowful year—I did not even mount a horse. I grew accustomed, contrary to my temperament, to complete solitude and silence, so that with the total interruption of scholarly interaction, I feared I might become melancholy <note>original: "melancholisch"; in the 17th century, this was viewed as a dangerous medical and spiritual imbalance caused by excessive black bile</note>.

The month of March, much to my great sorrow, snatched away David Steudlin, my companion from youth. I must relate something about him, so that the reports of this first half-year might contain something noteworthy.

A harsh misfortune befell my fellow citizens on August 15th. Poorly armed, they opposed a troop that intended to drive away their large and small livestock, but they were unequal in strength. Three died on the spot. The fourth—a wealthy merchant—succumbed later to his wounds, as did the fifth, after he had suffered cruel pains for fourteen days. Yet both were shamefully denied entry into Stuttgart, and the latter, in his own land, near Plochingen, had his baggage and horses of great value taken away by a band of robbers. He could scarcely save himself by means of his fast horse.

But so that I might do something nonetheless, while the leaders of the arts <note>original: "Musageten"; a classical reference to those who lead the Muses, here referring to the university or ecclesiastical directors.</note> hesitated (*), I applied all my effort to the restoration and preservation of the students of theology. For from the 1,046 individuals who were once destined for the Church among us, we have dwindled to only 338.

I do not remember having done anything else of significance, except that I assisted my people of Calw <note>Andreä had served as a superintendent in Calw before moving to Stuttgart; he remained a fierce advocate for the town, which had been devastated during the Thirty Years' War</note> with all possible loyalty and diligence, partly through intercession and partly through sharing advice (*). When I did this once in a cabinet meeting with the Prince on February 20th, I noticed well that I was making others ill-disposed toward me, because I seemed to be depriving them of their hoped-for plunder and insisted that one must keep one's given word. Thus, one is only popular when one nicely gives in—whether rightly or wrongly? That matters not—and one must either sacrifice one's conscience to remain in favor, or fall into disgrace. 

When Prince Christian <note>Christian of Württemberg (1639–1640), the short-lived son of Duke Eberhard III</note> was born, I was the first to express my joy and offer congratulations. In return, I received sixty <term>gulden</term> <note>a significant sum of currency</note> for the scholarship students in Tübingen as a reward.

The following year, 1640, a climacteric year <note>original: *Stufenjahr*; in early modern thought, certain years in a person's life—often multiples of 7 or 9—were considered critical "steps" or turning points for health and fortune</note> (*), became for me full of torment in body and soul. Through these same springs, my son Gottlieb also recovered from the wretched illness he had contracted due to the poor (††) food in the seminary <term>Stift</term> <note>the *Tübinger Stift*, the famous theological college in Württemberg where Andreä himself had studied</note>. —against me and my colleague Schüelin, raging from the pulpit, and he knew no end to the evils he spread at feasts and in the company of his own kind. He declared this a victory for his side and became so inflamed against me and Dr. Wagner <note>Tobias Wagner (1598–1680), a prominent Lutheran theologian and ally of Andreä</note> that he accused us of Weigelianism <term>Weigelianism</term> <note>the mystical and often controversial teachings of Valentin Weigel; in this era, it was a common "heresy" charge used to smear reformers who emphasized inner spirituality over rigid dogma</note> and slander; however, he received a reprimand for this and was forced to retract his lies. 

Throughout this entire affair, he revealed himself as a man of a fluent tongue but not of piety—venerable in his habit <term>habit</term> <note>clerical clothing or vestments</note> but unholy of heart, with a bold forehead and an impudent tongue. By his faction, he was an Epicurean; by his deeds, a Simoniac <term>Simoniac</term> <note>original: *Simoniaker*; referring to Simony, the practice of buying or selling church offices or spiritual favors</note>; in short, a man dangerous to the church. A large part of the year was spent on this dispute, which was very vexing to me, and the reasons for which will not be a matter of indifference for posterity to know.

Some—myself among them—believed that the improper dances, the all-too-frequent feasts, and the extravagant luxury of dress, amidst the ruin of the fatherland <note>a reference to the ongoing devastation of the Thirty Years' War (1618–1648)</note>...

Even those in whom one still expected to find a spark of piety mocked our zeal and yielded to those who felt it necessary to lull their guilty consciences to sleep through amusements. With such leaders, one surely hurries toward the abyss!

Meanwhile, I neglected nothing regarding the establishment, or the easing, or the restoration...

At this, I—having seen contrasting examples nearby <note>Andreä likely refers to other high-ranking court figures whose moral failings were well-known to him</note>—was almost astonished. At the very least, these testimonies awakened in me a great and rightful admiration for such virtues.

Even in the interim (*) I did not cease to attend to the affairs of the Church, especially when several miraculous signs <note>Original: "Wunderzeichen" — often interpreted in this era as celestial events or unusual occurrences seen as divine warnings</note> shook even the hardest of hearts. Finally, with the help of my colleague Schüelin, I established the long-sought and long-obstructed church discipline <term>Kirchencensur: A formal system of moral oversight and ecclesiastical discipline used by the Lutheran church to regulate the behavior of the congregation</term> against dissolute morals. We immediately made a warning example of an adulterer, although I feared not a little that our institution might be smothered at birth—since "the crows usually escape punishment" (†). I also drafted sumptuary laws <term>Aufwandsgesetze: Laws designed to curb extravagance and regulate private expenses on clothing, food, and social festivities to maintain social order and frugality</term> against luxury in clothing and banqueting—

Finally, on August 21st, the Ansbach wedding <note>The marriage of Margrave Albrecht II of Brandenburg-Ansbach to Henriette Louise of Württemberg-Mömpelgard</note> took place with a splendor that was, admittedly, restricted according to the circumstances of the time; nevertheless, twelve princely persons of both sexes and six counts were in attendance. For as kindly and generously as she was otherwise treated, she could not endure the falsity of the Calvinists, the terrible expressions used against the omnipresence of the body of Christ <note>A major point of theological conflict; Lutherans believed in the "Real Presence" (ubiquity) of Christ's body in the bread and wine, which Calvinists rejected</note>, the willful slanders against us, and the Vatinian hate <term>Vatinian hate: Derived from the Latin "Vatinianum odium," referring to an exceptionally intense, persistent, and visceral hatred, named after the Roman politician Publius Vatinius</term> directed at us. She therefore sought her recall in frequent letters to me and received it; she will likely abhor Calvinist faithlessness for the rest of her life.

Regarding friends I might have found during the time of my stay here (*) at the court and in the chancellery <note>The *Kanzlei* (Chancellery) was the administrative office where the Duchy's legal and political records were managed</note>, no one need ask—for in both places one finds friends enough—but they are the kind who are the first in flattery and the last in providing service. Yet, if my feelings do not deceive me, I must prefer Borken, from the Anhalt region; Stramelius, from Pomerania, once the tutor of the ruling prince; and Moriz Cronegk, from Carinthia, a Chamberlain, above all others. This last is a man who possesses not only old German loyalty <note>original: *alte teutsche Treue*; a phrase Andreä often uses to contrast perceived traditional German sincerity with the perceived superficiality of foreign courtly manners</note> and excellent qualities, but also Christian virtues. Would that he might show as much courage as he has a feeling for what is good and a strong voice, and take the best interests of the fatherland under his protection, even if it were to happen at the risk of his private fortune!

Since I am writing a private history, no one will blame me if I add something here regarding my physical temperament. It is weak and cannot tolerate the cold, but it can endure hard work. Without having to make use of a physician, I have been afflicted by only a few and brief illnesses up to my current age.

I love paintings and works of art, but I despise wealth. My table is modest and hospitable; my spirit is cheerful, calm, and free.

# Book Six.

### The following seven years in Stuttgart.
### From the Year 1643–1649.

---

When I decided to write this rhapsody <note>The author uses "rhapsody" here in the classical sense: a patchwork or miscellaneous collection of writings</note> of my life, I had a very different intention than I do now. At that time, my purpose was to defend my orthodoxy—which I paired with moral purity and candidness—against the bites of envy and slander; I noted the other events and accidents of my life on separate sheets. However, as the memory of the past was lost through the fire of the city <note>This refers to the catastrophic destruction of Calw in 1634, where Andreä lost his library, manuscripts, and belongings</note> along with my collections, I began to enter everything that happened afterward into these accounts, and to compose, as it were, a special diary for my own use. I believed I must remind the fault-finding reader of this, so that he does not complain that such minor circumstances are being forced upon him. As long as I live, let them be left to me! In the future, anyone may separate them from the record of my life story <note>original: *Lebensbeschreibung*</note> as they please! Now, after this explanation, I take up the thread again and continue, with God’s help.

The year 1643, which now followed <note>At age 57</note>, was a very sad one for our fatherland; for me, however—aside from a few minor stains—it flowed by cheerfully and peacefully. For the resentment of the powerful against me had largely subsided; the envy of my equals diminished, and those of lower rank followed their lead, ceasing their injustices toward me. My health was robust, and my wealth grew through the generosity of my Duke, August <note>August the Younger, Duke of Brunswick-Lüneburg (1579–1666), a celebrated scholar and founder of the Herzog August Library</note>. 2. All running around and canvassing for positions shall cease:
3. The freedom of votes shall be preserved:
4. The majority of the same shall decide:
5. It shall be permitted to hold a different opinion:
6. One person alone shall not abolish what has been decided:

### The Year 1645. <margin>Aged 59 years</margin>

The year 1645 (*) was for the most part burdensome to me due to physical ailments and a dryness of spirit <note>original: *Geistesdürre*; a term often used by scholars of this era to describe a period of intellectual exhaustion or "spiritual dryness"</note>. For the lack of digestion, from which I had suffered since the end of the previous year, plagued me greatly until May—though in such a way that I could dedicate the mornings to work, while in the afternoons I was afflicted by sharp abdominal cramps.

...there were so many examples before me of the most respected men from all estates who cast aside their crowns, bishop’s caps, miters <note>original: "Inseln," likely a transcription error for "Infuln," the liturgical headdress of a bishop</note>, scepters, fasces <note>term: "Fascen" (fasces); bundles of rods used in ancient Rome to symbolize a magistrate's power and jurisdiction</note>, robes of honor, purple gowns, footstools, treasures, and everything belonging to human pomp and pageantry, distancing themselves from such things so that they might dedicate themselves to religion, quietude, contemplation, and reading, and after so many years of labor, could either truly live, or learn how to do so. I believed that I, as an old warrior in my advanced years, with weakened health and wavering mental strength <note>original: "Seelenkräften," literally "soul-powers"</note>, was permitted to do this for my own sake—permitted to do so amidst the loss of relatives, friends, comrades-in-arms, and confidants, of whom I once saw so many around me, but now count so few—in these years, when I was tired of seeing and hearing so much vanity; and even more so, of taking part in it, as the trifles <note>original: "Spielwerke," literally "toy-works" or the "mechanics of play"</note> of men disgusted me—permitted to do so because of the role I once played on the world’s stage <note>original: "Schaubühne der Erde"</note>, not to my shame, but which now, with the change of scenery, is unpleasant, outdated, and loathed—finally, permitted to do so because of the great generosity of my lord, Duke August <note>August the Younger, Duke of Brunswick-Lüneburg (1579–1666), a famed scholar-prince and founder of the Herzog August Bibliothek</note>, which left me fearing neither hunger nor a bad reputation, so as to finally get out of the way of those to whom I had long been a nuisance and a hindrance in their evil deeds.

Thus, the terror and the absurd judgments of many people ended in laughter! (*)

These may be roughly the insignificant events of this period! # Seventh Book.
## Bebenhausen. <margin>The year 1650; at age 64.</margin>

Just as I believed I was steering toward the harbor of my release and had already reached the coast, a wind—I know not what kind, blowing from the north—drove me back out to the high seas to face new storms once more. For in the Jubilee year of 1650, when deliberations were held and resolutions passed regarding the restoration and expansion of the <term>Consistory<note>The Consistory was the central administrative and governing body of the Lutheran church in the Duchy of Württemberg.</note></term> and the <term>monastery schools<note>These were elite state-run boarding schools established in former Catholic monasteries to prepare talented boys for university and the clergy.</note></term>, <insert>Jacob</insert> Heerbrand received his requested discharge. I, too, was released from my duties at the court and the chancellery, yet the burden of the Abbey of Bebenhausen was laid upon my shoulders. I accepted the commission, though with hesitation, holding onto the hope that—should my strength fail to bear it—I might later exchange it for the more pleasant solitude of Hirsau <note>Hirsau was another major Benedictine monastery-turned-school; Andreae viewed it as a more peaceful retreat compared to the administrative duties at Bebenhausen.</note>.

Dr. Melchior Nicolai, who was called from Tübingen, was appointed to the office of Provincial Provost, which had stood vacant for eleven years <note>More precisely, fifteen years since the death of Daniel Hizler.</note>. Georg Bader was not entrusted with the office of <term>Preacher<note>original: "Prädikatur." This refers to a specific senior pastoral position, often associated with a cathedral or a major city church.</note></term> until the following year.

Before I departed from Stuttgart, I baptized Prince Karl Christoph on January 30th, who had been born two days prior. The actual baptismal ceremony, however, was not held until March 19th, accompanied by unusual pomp and feasting. This festivity was tragically disrupted by the unexpected death of the seven-year-old Princess, Dorothea Amalia, and the grief of the princely parents was doubled by the death of Prince Karl Christoph himself <note>The infant prince lived only a few months; his death in May 1650 effectively ended this branch of the family tree.</note>, which occurred moreover during their absence. These circumstances dealt the mother an incurable wound; they serve as a sobering proof that great sorrow and regret often follow excessive joy and extravagance.

On April 15th, I delivered my final sermon at court—which was the 1,070th I had given there. I took my leave the following day in a private audience with the Duke and traveled on the 25th to Bebenhausen, where I gave my first sermon three days later. As a colleague, I found Georg Linden

Though some storms tossed me about, they did not pull me under. I found the court gracious, faithful, and obliging beyond expectation. I can solemnly attest that I was never publicly insulted by the court through words or deeds—for who can avoid hidden wrongs?—and was, on the contrary, honored with many kindnesses, to which I confess myself a debtor and which I praise.

But how little did the Chancellery <term>Kanzlei: the central administrative and legal office of the Duchy</term>, and especially its ecclesiastical branch, support my hopes, my loyalty, or my love—how little did it defend my innocence, which it surely knew, against disgrace and slander! All of this, which originated from a single instrument of hell <note>Likely referring to a specific personal or political rival within the church administration</note> and is left to God's judgment, I would have borne with more composure had it not sometimes been linked to the detriment of Christianity and religion...

# Book Eight.
### Bebenhausen.
### From the Years 1651—1653.

The following year <note>1651, at the age of 65</note> initially flattered me with a favorable wind, offering relief from my labors and the pleasantness of solitude, which contributes so much to peace of mind and physical health. However, this joy was shorter and more fleeting than I had hoped. For although I often felt fear even when I was safe, I still could not escape the schemes of Simon <note>This likely refers to a specific adversary or perhaps a personification of "Simony"—the corrupt purchase of church offices—which Andreae fought against throughout his career</note>, which were only uncovered toward the end of the year. Thus, I learned the truth of the saying: in cultivated lands, one finds cattle and sheep, but in the wilderness, one finds wild, ravenous beasts.

Meanwhile, my Duke and Duchess <note>Duke Eberhard III of Württemberg and his wife, Anna Dorothea</note>, whom I attended in Tübingen on February 2nd and March 12th, remained graciously inclined toward me. Therefore, I set out for Calw on July 18th to seek medicine and to cheer my spirit, making use of the sedan chair that August <note>Possibly a reference to a family member or a high-ranking official who supported the author during his confinement.</note> had sent so that I could come to him. But, alas! How different I found this city! How greatly disfigured and distorted! For in the place of harmony, enmities and factions had arisen—in place of modesty, luxury and arrogance—in place of industriousness, idleness and ostentation; while piety, obedience, and care for the youth were clearly flagging. Therefore I returned, and on August 31st said my final farewell to Calw; strengthened in neither spirit nor body, although on the 25th I had the joy of attending a wedding anniversary, and on August 2nd celebrating the festival of my own marriage, now spanning forty years.

Upon my return home, I found my monastery "planted" with new students, who had entered on July 25th and whom I formally swore into their duties on September 6th. What has happened elsewhere, I did not learn in my Trophonian Cave <note>A classical reference to the Cave of Trophonius, an oracle where visitors were said to be struck with such awe or fear that they lost the ability to laugh; the author uses it here as a metaphor for his gloomy, isolated, and oppressive living conditions.</note>, and what occurred at the Diet of Regensburg <note>The "Reichstag" or Imperial Diet of the Holy Roman Empire, which met in 1653 to address the aftermath of the Thirty Years' War.</note> is beyond my sphere. Yet on July 31st, we celebrated a day of thanksgiving for the election of Ferdinand IV <note>Ferdinand IV (1633–1654) was elected King of the Romans in 1653, designating him as the successor to the Holy Roman Emperor, though he died of smallpox only a year later.</note>. <meta>This page continues the narrative from the previous page's conclusion of Andreae’s autobiography, transitioning from his personal prayers to a biographical account of his final months and death in 1654.</meta>

These are the words with which J. V. A. <note>Johann Valentin Andreae (1586–1654), the prominent Lutheran theologian and social reformer to whom this biography refers.</note> concludes his autobiography!

The following year, 1654, released him from Bebenhausen <note>A former Cistercian monastery in Württemberg where Andreae served as Protestant prelate and superintendent.</note>, but only to free him from all the world’s evils shortly thereafter. In February of that year, he was transferred to Adelberg as Abbot. Since he simultaneously became a member of the narrow committee of the regional estates <note>German: *engeren Landschaftsausschusses*. This was a powerful administrative body in the Duchy of Württemberg that managed taxes and regional governance.</note>, he was forced to travel back to Stuttgart as early as the following March 27th—a city that never suited him, and which would eventually see him die.

> “The last months of his life were but a struggle with death, which was finally decided on June 27th. (*) Toward the end of that time, he was visited by Anna Johanna, the sister of Duke Eberhard, and seven clergymen; joined with them, he commended his spirit into the hands of God. One half of his soul already hovered in heaven while the other still lingered with Duke August <note>August the Younger, Duke of Brunswick-Lüneburg (1579–1666). He was a great scholar and a devoted lifelong friend and patron of Andreae.</note>. At noon, he dictated a letter to this noble man and took up the pen to sign his name for the last time. He managed two letters; at the third, death stayed his hand.”

---

(*) Here I acknowledge an error I committed, as I wrote in the *Historical Pocketbook etc.* (Winterthur 1797, p. 294) that he had died as the Abbot of Bebenhausen.

<meta>This page concludes the account of Johann Valentin Andreae's death on June 27, 1654, following the description of his final moments and his last attempts to correspond with Duke August of Brunswick-Lüneburg.</meta>

“Thus lived and died the one of whom Jakob Spener <note>Philipp Jakob Spener (1635–1705), the influential founder of Lutheran Pietism, who deeply admired Andreae’s work on church reform.</note>, that dear man of God, used to say: ‘If I could raise anyone from the dead for the benefit of the church, it would be Valentin Andreae!’” (*)

On the thirtieth, he was laid to rest with a large following at the outer hospital cemetery, where the following epitaph <note>A commemorative inscription on a tomb or monument.</note> stands:

->To Jesus, the Savior of Mankind<-

Johann Valentin Andreae, Doctor of Sacred Theology, born in Herrenberg, son of Johannes, Abbot of Königsbronn, and grandson of Jakob <note>Jakob Andreae (1528–1590), a famous Lutheran theologian and primary author of the Formula of Concord.</note>, the incomparable theologian. Abbot of Adelberg, Counselor to both Prince August of Brunswick and Lüneburg and Eberhard of Württemberg, and a most highly deserving overseer of his homeland. After he had served the Church of Christ at Vaihingen for 6 years, Calw for 19 years, the court at Stuttgart for 11 years, and Bebenhausen for 4 years, by voice and example, in Christian literature and ecclesiastical discipline, with a heroic spirit and pen; having served for 50 years with all faithfulness and skill as a Man of God—an ornament of literature and the mechanical arts, and a truly regular theologian of orthodoxy—after 40 years of marriage and at the age of 67, on June 27, 1654, falling peacefully asleep in a death that mirrored his life, he was laid here to await the sound of God's trumpet. He is greatly missed.

## II.

### Johann Valentin Andreae’s testamentary ordinance, drawn up after the Fire of Calw in the year 1634.
<note>The town of Calw was brutally burned and looted by imperial troops in September 1634 during the Thirty Years' War. Andreae, who was the superintendent there, lost his home, his extensive library, and his collection of art and instruments.</note>

Just as the contemplation of death is appropriate at all times, the present moment calls me to it in a special way. God has deprived me of almost all earthly goods, while a plague rages all around among the people; He seems to summon me to prepare for death and to bring the end of my security <note>In this context, Andreae uses "security" to describe his mortal life or earthly safety.</note> closer to me. I therefore consider it my duty, and the duty of every Christian, to be resolved, and to meet the voice of the highest Ruler when He calls me away, undaunted...

...to be heard—then, since my estate <note>original German: "Vermögen." That the great God allowed me to be born honorably, raised uprightly, and instructed in good knowledge, I hold and confess as a great benefit—an even greater one, that I was initiated into the Christian religion, preserved within it, and received into the communion of saints; but for the greatest of all, that He chose me to be a member, indeed a proclaimer of the evangelical <note>In the context of 17th-century Germany, "evangelical" (evangelisch) specifically denotes the Lutheran faith.</note> religion and a dispenser of the divine mysteries <note>A traditional theological term for a minister who administers the Sacraments.</note>. Both, therefore, appear—and do not merely faithfully warn of the danger, but rather provide sure and wholesome counsel and means to oppose the encroaching heresies—and through me, they invite the most prominent men of Austria, whose sincerity and purity of religion are proven, to a union of designs. I attribute [the success of my mission] not to myself, but, after God, to Mr. von Hohenfelder <note>Baron Erasmus von Hohenfeld (1575–1638) was an influential Austrian nobleman and a staunch supporter of the Lutheran Church in Upper Austria.</note>. Through his prestige, my commission gained weight; through his wisdom, it found a path; and through his integrity, it gained respect among patriots; through his diligence, I was granted a hearing even amidst the most important affairs. Through his efforts, my discourse was more widely disseminated, and through his generosity, it was supported. I lived, as it were, in his pay, and spoke through his tongue. Christ, for whom he works, will reward him; the Prince <note>Referring to Johann Friedrich, Duke of Württemberg (1582–1628).</note>, whose virtues he praised, will love him; and the Württemberg Ministry, whose vigilance he recommended everywhere, will honor him. 

All people of Württemberg, whom he gladly welcomed like fellow countrymen, will surely visit him, and he will therefore be called the <term>Maecenas|A reference to Gaius Maecenas, the advisor to Roman Emperor Augustus and a famous patron of the arts; the term became a synonym for a wealthy and influential benefactor.</term> not only of religion and literature, which he already is, but also of the people of Württemberg. ### IV.
#### *) First Apparition.
An account of what I, Hans Keyl, citizen and inhabitant of Gerlingen <note>Gerlingen is a town located near Stuttgart in what was then the Duchy of Württemberg.</note>, saw in a vision on February 4 in the year 1658, and what was revealed to me by the same.

First, when I entered the vineyard, I read the morning blessing and further the Our Father, and prayed that God might one day deliver us from this <term>vale of tears|A traditional Christian metaphor for the hardships of earthly life, derived from the Latin 'vallis lacrimarum' in the Psalms.</term>; immediately thereafter, I saw a man standing before me in a white robe, who said to me: "The Lord give you a good day." But out of fear, I gave him no answer. Then He spoke: "Be comforted, your prayer has been heard by the Lord; I am an angel sent by God to you, so that you should declare to your Sovereign of Württemberg <note>Eberhard III, Duke of Württemberg (reigned 1628–1674).</note> that God intends to punish the land and the people because of great sin, if people will not do penance. For the Lord has visited the whole of Christendom now for twenty years <note>Though the Thirty Years' War ended in 1648, the speaker likely includes the subsequent years of recovery and localized conflicts as part of a single era of divine 'visitation.'</note> with war and bloodshed, hunger, famine, pestilence, ruin, and all kinds of punishments, but no one takes heed, rather it becomes worse every day." At this, the angel began to cry out: "Woe, woe!"

<summary>This page marks a shift from the memoirs of Johann Valentin Andreae to the recorded "First Apparition" of Hans Keyl, a peasant who claimed to have received a divine warning for the Duke of Württemberg regarding the need for repentance following the Thirty Years' War.</summary>
<keywords>Hans Keyl, Gerlingen, Württemberg, vision, angel, Thirty Years' War, repentance, divine punishment</keywords>

### 2) Second Apparition.
->Excerpt from the Protocol.<-

Yesterday, Monday, Keyhl came again in the morning to the Reverend Pastor and revealed with weeping eyes that because they would not believe him, an even greater wonder had occurred. For as he went again into his vineyard today in broad daylight, the aforementioned angel appeared again in the same form as before and addressed him thus: "God greet you, dear friend, have you declared and shown what I commanded you?" Whereat Keyhl was again greatly terrified and said that by order of the authorities <note>The *Obrigkeit* or local government often suppressed such "prophecies" to prevent civil unrest or political friction with the Duke.</note>, he had not been able to carry it out; whereupon the angel remarked: "That has already come before my Lord Jesus, therefore I am sent to you again; go hence, and say to the Pharaoh..." <note>A biblical reference to the stubborn ruler of Egypt; here, the angel uses it to describe the Duke of Württemberg, who refuses to listen to the divine warning.</note>

In Gerlingen, [the atmosphere was] sad and heavy-hearted. When we questioned Hans Keyhl himself, we found that his answer agreed with the Pastor’s report. Furthermore, this detail is noteworthy: a lake located right next to the aforementioned Gerlingen has recently acquired an unusually strong smell. Indeed, even at 30 paces away, we smelled the foul stench quite strongly. It tastes <note>The writer likely means "smells" or "perceives," though "schmäcken" in older German can refer to both taste and smell.</note> no different than the <term>Bollerbadwaßer; the mineral-rich sulfur water from the famous springs at Bad Boll, known for its potent "rotten egg" odor.</term>, though much stronger—or as if one were to ignite gunpowder and sulfur together, or smell a recently fired musket. However, we could not detect that the water itself possessed this smell, but rather we judge that it comes from elsewhere, especially since no fish in the lake have died off. May God, through His revealed Word, grant an improvement in our lives, so that we have no need for such direct visions. Dated Tuesday, February 8, in the year 1648.
